lines: Alex Kantrowitz and Ranjan Roy argue Big Tech's rough earnings week marks a shift: investors are moving from rewarding aggressive AI infrastructure spending to questioning whether that capex and the core businesses behind it are sustainable.

They say the web's old bargain, where search sends traffic to publishers in exchange for crawling, is breaking down as AI overviews answer queries directly, while closed ad ecosystems like Meta and Amazon look more resilient; the show notes Meta has overtaken Google in ad revenue.

On Anthropic's S-1, the hosts see a highly cash-efficient business but argue its margins are likely flattered by discounted compute from partners Amazon and Google, and that its employee equity is creating an unusual concentration of wealth.
They contend aggressive LLM price wars are commoditizing models, and that efficiency gains could reduce demand for massive data-center build-outs, with knock-on risk for data-center operators.
title: Big Tech's Ugly Week, Getting Rich At Anthropic, AI Costs Plunge

lines: Eve CEO Jay Madheswaran argues AI's real impact on plaintiff law is revenue expansion, not cost-cutting: firms are limited by legal labor rather than client demand, and the show says they turn away up to 96% of potential cases.
He says AI agents that run the full case lifecycle, from intake to settlement and often 10,000+ individual actions, can let firms handle up to five times more cases without proportional hiring.
In his view, legal software is really a 'shadow labor market', making its addressable market far larger than traditional software metrics suggest.

He argues insurers' centralized, automated claim-denial systems create a data asymmetry that AI-equipped plaintiff firms can now counter, with attorneys becoming data-scientist-like designers of agent workflows.
Madheswaran expects contingency law's outcome-based model to spread to other legal areas, and future firms to scale by hyper-specializing in specific fact patterns backed by proprietary data.
title: Why AI Could Turn Small Law Firms Into Billion-Dollar Businesses

lines: 本期与王恺聊江南秋季饮食，核心观点是“不时不食”：对食材在地性与季节性的讲究，既是农业社会传统的延续，也是对抗工业化饮食同质化的一种生活美学。
节目称传统苏州蟹宴重在蟹粉菜而非整蟹，因为在文人饮食体系里当众剥蟹被视为不雅；大闸蟹则因“清水养蟹”技术推广，从小而杂的野生蟹变成规格统一、品质可控的商品。
嘉宾认为蟹酿橙、炖生敲、西湖醋鱼等不少“古法名菜”，其实是上世纪80年代厨师依据古籍所做的复原与再创作，并非一脉相承。
在他看来，江南风味的深层逻辑是糟、酱、醉、腌、臭等发达的发酵技术；而一些地方饮食的“荒漠化”源于流量驱动的连锁扩张和预制菜，并非缺少好食材。
他还提到，好的市井小馆要看是否被本地资深食客长期青睐而非点评评分，顶尖厨师的共同点是坚持亲自挑选食材。
title: 512 与王恺漫话江南食事：从文人蟹宴到乡野土菜

lines: Thai Duong and Bruce Dang of hacking firm Calif argue AI is collapsing the window between finding a software flaw and exploiting it, so defenses built around patching and detection are no longer enough.

They say models good at coding and debugging are inherently good at hacking, so the offensive risk can't be separated from the productivity gains; the PHP2Shell bug, dormant in a language used by about 70% of websites, is their example.

In their view, AI agents can reverse-engineer public patches on GitHub into working exploits before users update, and attacks have shifted from surgical intrusions to mass compromises spreading at machine speed.

They claim AI analysis of long-hardened codebases turns up as many as ten times more vulnerabilities than previously estimated, while formal verification still can't scale to software as large and fast-changing as browsers.

Today's edge belongs to 'centaur' hackers pairing human intuition with AI, which they expect to be short-lived, and the attacker-defender asymmetry persists because defenders must cover every entry point while keeping systems running.
title: PHP2Shell Won't Be the Last Big AI Cybersecurity Risk

lines: The a16z team argues that America's defense, energy, manufacturing and robotics booms are converging into one story: rebuilding the domestic industrial base, which they frame as essential to national security and long-term competitiveness.

In their view, defense contracts act as a financial catalyst that effectively subsidizes industrial capacity later used by commercial sectors like robotics and medical devices, while private capital now funds systems ahead of government demand, bypassing the procurement 'valley of death'.

They say startups such as Mariana Minerals and Hadrian often must vertically integrate because legacy suppliers lack the agility and technology next-generation systems need, and that AI lets technicians reconfigure lines on the fly, making high-mix, low-volume manufacturing economical.

The hosts describe a new class of 'co-engineering' suppliers that rethink subcomponents rather than just executing old specs, and argue the grid must shift from static mechanical designs to software-native power electronics.

They also contend physical-world companies are drawing the most ambitious founders, and that bringing local communities into the economic upside is key to winning public support for new infrastructure.
title: The Startups Rebuilding American Industry | The AD50

lines: Bridgewater CEO Nir Bar Dea argues the world has moved from a century of globalization into an era of nationalism, with countries prioritizing self-reliance and keeping capital at home.
He says Bridgewater now uses AI not just to execute trades but to generate investment ideas, producing insights that differ from what its human analysts would come up with.
Bar Dea warns that high US debt and deficits have used up much of the policy buffer, so any negative shock could hit households and companies harder than in the past.
He calls for AI regulation, citing three risks: misuse by bad actors, loss of control over more capable systems, and labor displacement he puts at up to 18% of the American workforce.

On leadership, drawing on six years in the Israeli military, he favors process over individual opinion, treating being wrong as the main way to learn, and hiring fast learners from non-traditional backgrounds.
title: Nir Bar Dea

lines: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman argues that teams of collaborating AI agents, not one monolithic superintelligence, scale better and are easier to keep aligned, making them the more resilient path forward.

On security, he says models now find vulnerabilities (such as critical PHP bugs) faster than humans can patch them, so the real task is re-architecting systems; he calls sandboxing superhuman models unsolved and points to deep alignment and activation monitoring instead.

He frames AI capital allocation as compute allocation: giving researchers unconstrained compute and leaning on test-time compute and chain-of-thought is what produces breakthroughs like OpenAI's internal Navier-Stokes proof experiments, which he admits brings some nostalgia for manual research.

Altman says personal agents have not yet had their 'Macintosh moment' because they lack reliability, but expects commerce to shift from web forms to agents acting for users; tokens stay the pricing unit because customers want cost predictability over outcome-based pricing.
title: Why Sam Altman is against a single superintelligence

lines: Barclays' Alex Altmann argues the AI trade is in a 'denial phase': sentiment stays overwhelmingly bullish even as financing stress builds at the edges of the build-out.

He sees a widening split between cash-rich hyperscalers and peripheral 'neoclouds' that are finding debt markets harder to tap, as AI capex — potentially reaching around 12% of GDP by some projections — competes for finite capital.

Altmann describes a 'KOSPI-fication' of the S&P 500, with roughly 75% of expected earnings growth concentrated in semiconductors and the wider AI ecosystem, and says the shifting beta of the 'AI factor' makes it hard for multi-manager funds to hedge.
He notes semiconductor stocks trade on very low multiples (he cites about 3x P/E), signaling investors believe the sector is at a cyclical peak rather than a secular inflection.

In his view, the next leg up needs a killer consumer application, since enterprise revenue alone can't justify multi-trillion-dollar valuations, while running large models locally on consumer hardware could reduce reliance on centralized data centers.
title: What Wall Street Really Thinks About the AI Trade Now

lines: Kyle Grieve and Shawn O'Malley argue Airbnb has become a capital-light, high-margin toll booth on global travel, and that its slowdown looks more like groundwork for the next growth phase than a peak.

They point to gross booking value compounding at 34% since 2024 and first-time bookers at a four-year high, with a moat built on about 500 million reviews and 200 million verified identities that capital alone can't replicate.

Growth levers they highlight include hotel inventory as an acquisition funnel (35% of first-time hotel guests book a home within a year) and India growing about 60% a year, while sponsored-listing revenue is delayed as management prioritizes AI-driven search.
The hosts credit 'founder mode' with doubling revenue on a roughly pre-pandemic headcount, and say revenue now outgrows stock-based comp, with strong free cash flow funding aggressive buybacks.
They treat regulatory crackdowns in New York and Barcelona as local headwinds given 9 million listings across 220 countries, while flagging cyclical travel risk and AI-agent competition.
podcast: The Investor's Podcast (We Study Billionaires)  - The Investor’s Podcast Network
title: TIP856: Airbnb (ABNB): The Business Outgrew Its Peak, The Stock Hasn't w/ Kyle Grieve & Shawn O'Malley

lines: Wharton professor Ethan Mollick argues AI has a large 'capability overhang': today's tools could already transform the economy, but organizational inertia keeps their impact far below what the technology allows.

He says individual workers see big productivity gains, yet companies lag because they lack 'multiplayer' processes to absorb high-volume AI output into team workflows, and have lost the muscle memory for redesigning roles and mandates.

In his view, reasoning models that think on a scratchpad before answering, plus agentic harnesses that let AI operate computers, have moved the technology from passive chat to multi-step task execution.

Mollick notes some large firms already earn positive ROI by using models as 'super-analysts' to find internal inefficiencies and launch new products, and expects falling token costs to make today's budget worries moot.
He warns AI tutors help when they scaffold learning but cause de-skilling when used to skip the effort that real learning requires.
title: This AI Expert Argues We're Underestimating AI's Productivity Impact — With Ethan Mollick

lines: Mark Cuban argues US healthcare's core problem is missing price discovery and broken incentives, and that AI alone won't fix it; transparency is the most effective disruptive tool.

His immediate advice for employers: run every benefits contract through AI before signing to expose hidden fees and intercompany transfers, which he calls 'contractual terrorism' by vertically integrated carriers steering plans to their own high-cost subsidiaries.

He says Cost Plus Drugs' public, low-markup pricing has pushed incumbents to cut prices even without direct deals, and proposes mandatory disclosure of taxpayer-funded contracts and letting cheaper out-of-network care count toward deductibles.

Cuban sees modular, trailer-sized manufacturing pods enabling local production of sterile injectables and personalized 'end-of-one' therapies, with DNA-based medicine becoming a subscription service as AI pushes drug design costs toward zero.
He expects doctors to become physician-scientists using AI on patient-specific data, and argues companies need C-suites that understand how models work to stay competitive.
title: Mark Cuban’s Plan to Make Healthcare Affordable

lines: United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby argues long-term capital bets beat short-term Wall Street metrics, pointing to United's large fleet expansion during COVID while rivals shrank.

He sees fast low-Earth-orbit Wi-Fi via Starlink as the industry's biggest differentiator, made possible by moving reservation software, seatback entertainment and other core systems in-house onto a modern tech stack.
Kirby says money-losing 'strategic' routes with no path to profit should be cut, and rejects customer surveys and expert consensus as poor predictors of how people actually behave.
He argues AI's real value is in speeding up programming and automating real-time decisions, and that showing customers data like radar maps during weather delays sharply improves satisfaction.
In his view, air traffic control modernization is the single biggest capacity bottleneck, held back by political incentives to keep scattered facilities.
title: The airline CEO putting Starlink on every plane

lines: Alpha School founder Joe Liemandt argues AI learning engines let students master the standard curriculum in about two hours a day, and the freed time should go to agency, teamwork, entrepreneurship and leadership rather than more academics.

He says engagement peaks when students are kept at roughly 80–85% correct — hard enough to require effort but not so hard they disengage — and that demanding challenges like MBA-level simulations make young students happier than simplified content.
The guests liken AI's impact on education to the tractor's arrival in 1910, which made traditional career paths obsolete and forced institutions to restructure.
They argue entrepreneurship is a teachable, repeatable skill set, and that universities fail mainly because they are built around adults and faculty rather than student success.
In their view, AI turns students from passive consumers into builders of software and products, and direct access to accomplished people makes high achievement feel attainable.
title: Reinventing School for the AI Era | Joe Liemandt, Gagan Biyani & Erik Torenberg

lines: 清华大学副教授袁先欣以2016年在伦敦政经学院重见天日的费孝通英文小说手稿《茧》为线索，认为它展示了费孝通社会学家身份之外，用文学探索中国农村工业化与社会改良的一面。
嘉宾认为30年代江南农村危机不只是“封建剥削”，而是大萧条背景下银本位货币制度与国际丝价波动共同造成的城乡经济循环断裂；与茅盾《春蚕》的左翼革命叙事不同，《茧》对农村出路给出了改良式设想。
小说中制丝工厂管理和女工生活的细节，取材于费孝通二姐费达生的蚕丝业改革实践；节目也借此重新评价费达生、朱玉宝等女性知识分子在实业救国和劳工福利中的核心作用。
嘉宾指出，费孝通转向社会学，深受大革命失败后社会性质论战和兄长投身革命的情感影响；而写《茧》的动机之一，是赛珍珠《大地》走红后西方对中国题材的兴趣。
节目还比较了关中与江南农村在土地占有、宗族形态和金融化程度上的差异，认为这解释了不同作家对“农村问题”的认知分歧。
title: 511 重新发现费孝通：文学视角下的三十年代江南丝业危机与北平青年思潮

lines: CAS Investment Partners founder Cliff Sosin argues intelligence has hard limits: it is a ratio for predicting complex dynamic systems, not an unbounded quantity, since reality often requires real-world experimentation.

As intelligence gets cheap, he says value shifts to its complements — proprietary data, human attention, physical proximity and scale, and emotional attachment — and investors should favor businesses that use them to lower costs or improve customer outcomes.

He expects most intelligence tasks to commoditize with rapid price deflation, leaving frontier models valuable only in a narrow set of use cases, and describes a U-shaped demand curve where falling prices eventually stop generating new usage.

He views the AI infrastructure build-out as a speculative but efficient redeployment of capital, like past industrial booms, while warning of overcapacity and a 'winner's curse' that makes picking winners hard.
Sosin also says AI-driven portfolio construction is outperforming humans on sizing, and argues education must stay bimodal: build foundational skills without models so people can direct them well.
podcast: Invest Like the Best with Patrick O'Shaughnessy
title: Cliff Sosin - Owning the Complements to Intelligence - [Invest Like the Best, EP.497]

lines: Axios's Dan Primack frames Anthropic's S-1 as a referendum on the AI business model and a test of whether markets can fund Anthropic, SpaceX and Meta's capital needs at the same time; he argues investors will buy in regardless of risk factors to own a piece of the foundational layer.
Per the filing as discussed, revenue rose from $41 million three years ago to $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, with revenue per employee climbing from $1.4 million to $6.6 million.
Revenue per dollar of compute reportedly rose from $0.40 in early 2025 to $2.08, credited largely to Claude Code and Claude Cowork, and no single customer now exceeds 10% of revenue.

The episode highlights the unusual inclusion of catastrophic-harm risk factors in an S-1, and notes that despite $141 billion raised, no investor owns more than 5%, leaving no concentrated shareholder control.
Primack sees Anthropic's early B2B focus as a key edge in a segment rivals underestimated while chasing consumers.
title: Emergency Pod: Anthropic's S-1 IPO Filing — With Dan Primack

lines: 上海交大教授陆铭认为，人口向大城市集聚是提升效率的经济规律，AI时代服务业占比上升、面对面交流需求增加，反而会强化中心城市的吸引力。
他认为汽车等行业的“内卷”源于地方政府招商引资的恶性竞争，以牺牲国内劳动者福利和环境为代价，变相补贴了海外消费者。
陆铭称大城市高房价很大程度上来自建设用地指标管制造成的人为供给短缺；县域竞争早期有助资本积累，如今已演变为市场分割和重复建设，需转向统一大市场。
在消费上，他认为劳动时间过长压抑了服务消费，主张限制工时、放开服务业管制，并配合公共服务均等化和税制改革来释放内需。
他还主张AI时代教育应从记忆、演算等技能转向通识教育，培养审美、价值观和对人性的理解，并呼吁建立解释中国央地关系的新经济学研究范式。
title: Vol.239 访问思考者1｜李翔对话陆铭：聊聊AI、内卷、房价和消费抉择

lines: OpenAI's Ari Weinstein and James Sun argue computer-using agents now work faster than the average human, and that the next step — superhuman speed — will change how people interact with software.

They frame the screen itself as a universal interface: agents can automate legacy enterprise systems that never got APIs, with standards like WebMCP helping agents and humans share the same interfaces.
They say cutting 'thinking tokens' drives both speed and reliability for OpenAI's Astra model, and that small gains — say from 97% to 99% task success — matter a lot for enterprise trust.

Enterprise adoption, in their view, needs deterministic sandbox controls plus configurable human-in-the-loop review, while the best workflows shift toward proactive background agents that fix issues before people notice.
They expect traditional UIs to survive because people like direct manipulation, and see the startup opportunity in vertical tools that stitch together non-API legacy systems.
title: OpenAI: When AI Agents Use Computers Faster Than You

lines: 《中国菜市场》作者、中山大学副教授钟淑如认为，菜市场不只是买菜的地方，而是城市里连接自然、地方文化与人际关系的“关系基础设施”。
她指出电商和超市的工业化供应链追求标准化与高周转，会过滤掉产量不稳、卖相差但风味独特的本地品种，让餐桌趋于同质化，也遮蔽了食物的产地和季节感。
菜市场接纳这些非标商品，扮演“补位者”角色；摊主作为“食物的人证”，靠长期信任网络维系社区生态，他们追求的“自由”是对生活节奏的掌控，代价是高强度、全年无休的劳动。
节目还谈到食物消费的阶级属性：高端农夫市集带有中产符号，传统菜市场则是少数高性价比、能容纳各类人群的公共空间。
嘉宾认为“过日子”的关键是建立自己的在地供应商网络，把吃饭从单纯摄入变成与地方、季节共振的日常练习。
title: 既然都争当「过日子人」，那一起去逛菜市场吧！

lines: Lindsay Owens, author of Gouged, argues retail pricing has shifted from fixed price tags to algorithmic 'surveillance pricing' that targets each shopper's maximum willingness to pay.

She says firms use proxies like location, device and browsing behavior for statistical discrimination that sidesteps anti-discrimination rules, and that algorithmic tools also enforce price conformity across franchises and independent retailers.
In her view, AI shopping agents such as Meta's Muse often push sponsored or higher-margin products, a conflict of interest that persists unless agents carry fiduciary duties.

Owens argues buyer and seller agents fighting each other creates deadweight loss without moving the final price, effectively reviving a time-consuming haggling era after 150 years of transparent pricing.
She notes consumers stay largely inelastic despite complaining about price hikes, and that some retailers now earn nearly a third of operating income from data-driven revenue.
title: AI Agents Are Already Changing the Price of Goods

lines: Scott Ramsower, who runs private equity funds at the $250 billion Teacher Retirement System of Texas, argues continuation vehicles are inherently conflicted because the GP is both seller and buyer, so every deal needs bespoke scrutiny of pricing, process and alignment.

He warns CVs and NAV loans can produce 'synthetic' DPI that flatters track records, and that routinely moving top assets into CVs strips commingled funds of the right-tail upside that drives PE returns.
He sees a growing pile of 'zombie funds' that can neither exit assets nor raise new capital, which will absorb LP governance time and drag on industry performance.

Ramsower argues semi-liquid retail PE products undermine the asset class's core edge, since illiquidity protects long-term value creation, and that fee-paying CVs cannibalize the fee-free co-investment flow LPs built over decades.
His answer is 'craftsmanship alpha': pairing quantitative diligence with a qualitative read of GP partnership cohesion that tends to crack when performance slips.
podcast: Capital Allocators – Inside the Institutional Investment Industry
title: Continuation Vehicles from the LP Seat – Scott Ramsower (EP.523)

lines: Paul Kedrosky argues the AI capex boom is uniquely dangerous because it combines four classic crisis drivers at once: loose credit, data-center real estate speculation, a transformative-technology narrative and US–China arms-race spending.
He says AI capex accounts for 25%–60% of quarterly US GDP growth, masking weakness elsewhere and distorting the usual read on economic health.
Unlike earlier general-purpose technologies that complemented labor, he sees AI as a substitute for white-collar symbolic work, implying faster, broader labor disruption.

He flags fragile demand: roughly 70% of frontier-lab revenue comes from about eight companies, and debt-financed buildouts could end in a Japan-style balance-sheet recession where rate cuts lose traction.
For analysts, he argues basic modeling is now a commodity; human value shifts to spotting inflections and tail events, since models drift toward the center of the distribution.
title: The Most Dangerous Investment Cycle In History | Paul Kedrosky

lines: Box CEO Aaron Levie argues AI agents let teams of 3–10 people match the output of organizations about 20 times their size, eroding incumbents' resource advantage as founders shift from doing the work to orchestrating and reviewing agents.
As execution costs like code and marketing assets approach zero, he says value moves to strategic clarity, product taste and spotting real market opportunities.

Cutting the cost of labor-heavy work by 90%+ creates demand for services that weren't economical before; in his view AI's ROI is currently far higher in high-stakes enterprise tasks than in consumer apps.

He sees a 'matrix' of opportunities in specialized agents for every job function in every industry, best built by pairing technical founders with domain experts — but stresses distribution and owning the customer relationship still decide who wins.
title: The New Startup Playbook | Box CEO Aaron Levie

lines: Revisiting Shopify 15 months after passing on it near $80, the hosts say the business has beaten their expectations — it now handles about 14% of US e-commerce — but they still won't buy at roughly 112x operating earnings.

They credit a flywheel of enterprise wins, high merchant retention and a rising take rate, and note the shift from heavy dilution to buybacks that now offset stock-based compensation, marking it as a self-funding compounder.

On agentic commerce, they argue Shopify's structured, real-time Catalog feed lets AI agents read product data more reliably than web scraping, and that intent-based AI discovery favors long-tail independent brands over big incumbents.

They push back on the idea that merchants will vibe-code their own replacements, citing operational complexity and lost perks like volume-negotiated payment rates, and see AI agents mattering more for high-consideration purchases than automated replenishment.
podcast: The Investor's Podcast (We Study Billionaires)  - The Investor’s Podcast Network
title: TIP855: Shopify (SHOP): The Big Winner of Agentic Commerce? w/ Shawn O'Malley & Daniel Mahncke

lines: Ben Horowitz argues that AI makes companies easier to start, but the hardest parts of founding — deciding under uncertainty, building momentum and managing self-doubt — haven't changed.
He frames AI as a "probabilistic computer" with instant utility, letting small teams reach huge audiences without the slow, network-dependent adoption curve of the early internet.
He rejects the "GPT wrapper" critique: serious apps combine multiple models and accumulate proprietary data, which becomes a durable moat alongside market dominance.
In his view, VC's real value today is generating momentum through hiring and customer wins rather than product advice, and AI entertainment is a new medium, not automated film or TV.
His advice for crises: founders need a sense of inevitability to push through doubt, and should ignore the overwhelming implications and focus only on the single best available move.
title: What It Takes to Win as a Founder | Ben Horowitz

lines: Richard Mott, owner of Chicago's North Pond and Spark Shared Kitchen, explains why restaurants are a brutal business: thin margins, volatile food and labor costs, and fleeting popularity, with fine dining operating as a high-stakes luxury product.

He argues operators face competition from "non-economic" owners who run restaurants for ego or lifestyle, and that following labor, overtime and immigration rules puts compliant players at a 5–10% cost disadvantage.

Mott says wine sales, historically fine dining's highest-margin line, are down about 25%, a consumer shift that threatens the traditional profit model; with no lag between input costs and revenue, restaurants must reprice often under inflation.

His answer is the shared-kitchen model, which pools licensing, equipment and compliance costs so small food entrepreneurs can start without heavy capital — and he credits 80% of a venture's success to the team, only 20% to the idea.
title: How a Chicago Restaurant Has Stayed Open For Nearly Three Decades

lines: The hosts argue AI spending is dangerously concentrated: about 1% of companies account for 90% of it, and most of that comes from unprofitable, VC-backed startups recycling capital — a circular loop without broad enterprise adoption, echoing Ken Griffin's bubble warning.

With Palo Alto Networks' Nikesh Arora, they frame the PHP exploit as a symptom of deep technical debt; AI has turned cyber defense into an automated cat-and-mouse game won by whoever can aggregate infrastructure data and spot anomalies at scale.

They say large enterprises are moving toward open-weight models for data sovereignty and auditability, and that autonomous agents in finance need a liability framework separating user error from platform failure.

On France's unrest, the hosts argue public spending above 50% of GDP fails to deliver quality services and fuels populist anger; they advocate shifting from defined-benefit programs to market-based equity models and selective, productivity-focused immigration.
title: AI Cyber Panic, Ken Griffin’s Bubble Warning, The Fall of France?

lines: The panel argues Google is betting on frontier models over near-term cloud profits, and is pushing toward a single, agent-first assistant that sits across its sprawling product lineup.

In that “headless” future, a unified agent replaces siloed app interfaces, so success gets measured by agentic query volume rather than classic user engagement; the core bottleneck is how Sundar Pichai splits scarce compute between Cloud revenue and research.
On funding, the hosts see AI moving from open-ended optimism to hard scrutiny, with investors showing fatigue after repeated mega-rounds and asking where personal agents make money.

Alex Stamos calls this a cybersecurity “Black October”: a critical PHP flaw exposed roughly 70% of websites to remote code execution, amid a surge of automated, AI-enhanced attacks he sees as a permanent shift.

He argues professionalized access brokers now use agents to find, secure and auction footholds, and that the fix is refactoring legacy stacks like PHP and Node.js into memory-safe languages — newly feasible with AI coding — plus better password hygiene.
title: Google’s Potential, AI Money Spigot Shutting?, PHP Bug & Cybersecurity’s “Black October”

lines: Andy Jassy says AI demand is unlike anything Amazon has seen: AWS's AI business hit a $25B run rate in three years, and even with about $220B of capex, 2026–27 capacity is largely sold out.
He expects power, cooling and chip constraints to last several years, and argues broad enterprise adoption needs inference costs to fall by an order of magnitude.
Custom silicon such as Graviton and Trainium is, in his view, a necessity for price-performance because dominant chip suppliers have little incentive to cut prices.

Inside Amazon, AI lets small cross-functional teams do in weeks what took dozens of people a year, so he favors versatile engineers over narrow specialists and is rebuilding products like Alexa from scratch.
He also says AI-speed vulnerability discovery means apps must be patchable by agents in minutes, and likens data center buildouts to the 1950s US highway program.
title: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy on Why Amazon Is Investing $220 Billion in AI

lines: 学者汪玉姣以泰国为切入点，梳理1850至1990年代侨批业的兴衰：这是一套“银信合一”、集汇兑、物流和跨国贸易于一体的去中心化商业网络，在没有现代金融设施的年代靠宗族关系把钱和信从曼谷经香港送到汕头。
嘉宾指出，批局的主要利润并非手续费，而是汇率差套利，以及把沉淀的汇款资金拿去做贸易周转；联号式的分散结构让它在战争和政策动荡中能及时止损、灵活迁移。
她认为泰国对华人以“吸纳”为主，通过改名、泰语教育等强制泰化把华人变成泰国公民，与周边国家的激进排华不同；二战“泰日同盟”时期业者仍维持了秘密汇路。
随着侨眷经济自立、现代金融下沉和通讯进步，侨批的“生存纽带”功能消失，90年代退出历史，部分批局转型旅行社，反映需求从生存汇款转向寻根探亲。
title: 510 泰国侨批沉浮录：下南洋浪潮中的跨国华人经济网络

lines: Jeanna Smialek, author of The Invisible Hand of Maria Edgeworth, argues the Regency-era novelist spread Adam Smith's ideas to the public by weaving them into fiction.
She says Edgeworth engaged critically with David Ricardo in letters, questioning comparative advantage and the risks of agricultural over-specialization in Ireland.
During the potato famine, Edgeworth shifted from strict laissez-faire toward what Smialek frames as proto-Keynesian intervention.

In Smialek's telling, economics' 19th-century turn to math ('physics jealousy') erased narrative-driven women thinkers, and today's AI disruption echoes the social instability of the early Industrial Revolution.
title: The Forgotten Godmother of Economic Literature

lines: a16z is broadening a16z crypto into a16z Frontier, backing ambitious, cross-disciplinary founders in hardware, science and media rather than investing by category; the hosts say founders should now ask whether an idea is ambitious enough, not too ambitious.

They argue AI lets small teams build full-stack companies spanning software, hardware and science that once took large organizations decades, and that the gap between AI-native startups and incumbents is the widest in tech history.
Open-source models are framed as the key safeguard against AI power concentrating in a few companies or governments.
They expect the internet to shift from human-to-human to agent-to-agent networks, while AI answers break the search-traffic bargain behind web content, forcing new economics and protocols.
Other ideas: AI reverse engineering makes hardware programmable, and adoption splits by age, with people over 35 tending to see new tech as a threat.
title: The Frontier Ideas a16z Wants to Fund | Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz & Chris Dixon

lines: Magic Patterns CEO Alex Danilowicz argues that as AI speeds up the final production stage, design work shifts toward brainstorming and exploring ideas as interactive, code-backed prototypes rather than static 2D mockups.

He says the product's canvas interface lets non-designers iterate on many directions at once instead of being locked into a linear chat thread, and that the company built it to solve a pain point its front-end-engineer founders had themselves.

The episode critiques the 'vibe-coded' look of many AI startup sites: heavy animation, scroll-jacking and hidden calls to action that obscure the product and hurt conversion; for AI apps, a visible prompt box on the landing page is framed as a key conversion driver.

Other points: privacy and data-retention transparency is becoming a prerequisite for trust, every role should do customer support, and staying differentiated means repeatedly reworking the product around new standards like MCP.
title: How To Stand Out In A World Of AI Designs

lines: Bhaskar Sunkara, co-author of The Blueprint, makes the case for market socialism: worker-managed firms, public banking and an expanded public sector, with markets still coordinating consumer goods.

He argues it fixes 20th-century socialism's flaws through hard budget constraints that let failing firms die, and benchmark wages that push firms toward productivity and tech investment instead of cheap labor.

On housing, he proposes public land ownership and state-led construction to bypass zoning barriers, while keeping rent differences based on demand; managers would be rewarded through performance pay and profit-sharing.
He says AI can't replace markets in coordinating constantly shifting preferences, and names the transition from existing property structures and short election cycles as the main obstacles.
title: Bhaskar Sunkara Thinks the Market Has a Place Under Socialism

lines: Intapp's Ben Harrison argues that "firm AI" in professional services is moving from research assistants to agents that carry out a firm's own multi-step procedures, such as fundraising, LP onboarding and deal lifecycle management.

Unlike general frontier models, he says, these agents plug into internal systems and draw on the firm's institutional memory and relationship data, while enforcing information barriers and confidentiality rules.
He sees governance, not model capability, as the main adoption barrier, and says firms with mature data and digital infrastructure can "skip the line."
In his view, automating junior analysts' data-heavy work lets firms scale without adding support staff, expanding margins and reshaping the apprenticeship model, while humans keep final decisions.
podcast: Capital Allocators – Inside the Institutional Investment Industry
title: AI in the Investment Firm – Ben Harrison (EP.522)

lines: In this sponsored replay, DealCloud's Ben Harrison argues that dealmakers need vertical software, because horizontal CRMs are built for linear sales funnels rather than multi-year relationship networks.

He says the biggest gain is automated data capture from email, calendars and third-party market data, replacing manual entry; generative AI then becomes a recommendation engine that flags likely deal targets.
He notes middle-market companies ($25M–$1B revenue) make up two-thirds of US PE deal value, and says Excel and legacy in-house systems remain DealCloud's main competitors.
He calls private equity and credit a secular bull market and cites projections of the asset class topping $20 trillion as retail access widens.
podcast: Capital Allocators – Inside the Institutional Investment Industry
title: [REPLAY] DealCloud - Ben Harrison (Dealcloud), (S3. Sponsored Insight)

lines: BCG chief economist Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak argues the idea that Gen Z and Millennials are falling behind is wrong: at the same life stage they have higher real incomes and stronger balance sheets than Boomers and Gen X.
He calls the K-shaped economy story statistically unsupported, saying the bottom of the income distribution has also gained in real income and net worth since 2020.

On housing, he says Millennial homeownership catches up with Gen X by about age 42, and a constant-size median home has been roughly as affordable for three decades; much of the squeeze reflects a preference for expensive cities.

He blames the pessimism on social media inflating benchmarks (such as the belief that $600K a year is needed), election cycles and weaker community networks, which feed 'financial nihilism' and spending over saving.
title: Why Younger Generations Are Convinced They Are Falling Behind | Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak

lines: The hosts pitch GE Aerospace as a near-monopoly in commercial jet engines with a huge installed base, whose profits come mainly from the aftermarket rather than new engines.
They describe a razor-and-blade model: engines are sold around break-even, while services and spare parts make up over 70% of revenue and most profits, with returns on invested capital near 40%.
Regulatory certification locks suppliers in for decades, and mandated maintenance plus the need for original parts make the aftermarket captive and more resilient than new-equipment sales.

They credit CEO Larry Culp's breakup of the old GE conglomerate and operational focus, citing the pieces' combined value rising from $96B to over $600B in eight years, and in-house castings to ease supply bottlenecks.

The main risk, in their view, is valuation: at about 40x free cash flow despite a $210B backlog, the stock is exposed to slower Boeing/Airbus output, normalizing maintenance cycles and multiple compression; the segment's profit fell 82% in 2020.
podcast: The Investor's Podcast (We Study Billionaires)  - The Investor’s Podcast Network
title: TIP854: GE Aerospace: Chris Hohn’s Biggest Bet w/ Daniel Mahncke & Shawn O'Malley

lines: IBM's Arvind Krishna and Palo Alto Networks' Nikesh Arora warn that quantum computing could break today's encryption by around 2030, so the move to post-quantum cryptography must start now to counter 'harvest now, decrypt later' attacks.
The guests expect 75–90% of enterprise token use to go to cheaper, auditable open-weight models, with frontier models reserved for high-stakes tasks.

They see a return to vertical integration, IBM- or Nvidia-style, and argue that thousands of separate software vendors create an unmanageable attack surface, driving consolidation onto a few platforms as AI makes many point tools redundant.

On security and policy, they call for pooled vulnerability data to reach parity with attackers, describe the global AI race as one no country will slow, and say agentic coding still can't be fully verified for high-reliability uses like banking.
title: Arvind Krishna & Nikesh Arora: Quantum Threat, Open vs Frontier AI, AI Cyber Warfare & SaaS Collapse

lines: Reducto CEO Adit Abraham argues that documents — PDFs, spreadsheets, scans — are the missing infrastructure layer holding AI agents back from real-world work.

He says frontier models look precise but have poor recall on long or complex files, silently dropping data in ways generic benchmarks don't catch; traditional OCR fares worse on nested tables and odd layouts.

Reducto's answer is specialized vision-language models plus self-correcting harnesses for deterministic, high-fidelity extraction, now extended to context-aware reasoning and document editing, with over 7 billion pages processed.

He sees a market opening because big labs compete on general reasoning, leaving the document 'last mile' to specialists; the episode cites 80% of insurance claim appeals being overturned as evidence of costly manual errors.
Abraham dismisses public benchmarks as marketing and recommends evaluating on domain-specific data with LLM-as-judge rubrics.
title: The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agents: Documents | Reducto’s Adit Abraham

lines: Nobel laureate James Robinson (Why Nations Fail) argues that political institutions determine economic outcomes: inclusive rules channel energy into innovation, while extractive ones enrich narrow elites.
He says the US is not a failed state but faces a crisis of inclusion, noting real incomes for the non-college majority have stagnated for about 50 years, alongside polarization and falling trust.
Robinson views China's boom as 'extractive growth' that he expects to stall, since the lack of political accountability eventually chokes off creative destruction.

He frames AI as an Industrial Revolution-style shock where productivity gains may displace unskilled wages, making distribution the central political problem; he cites South Korea as a model of accountable industrial policy.
He also defends trade unions as a check on employer monopsony power and says ideas about legitimacy shape state behavior as much as material interests.
title: James Robinson on What It Looks Like When a State is Failing

lines: 科沃斯 CEO 钱程谈“创二代”接班：难点在于把父辈那个时代的成功要素，转化成能穿越周期的新竞争力，推动公司从制造根基走向创新驱动和全球化。
他认为战略能否落地，取决于能否和组织里沉淀几十年的文化与执行习惯（“神经系统”）对接；组织变革不能照搬西方管理理论，要靠制度和信任逐步从“人治”走向体系化。
在竞争上，他认为消费电子没有永久护城河，品牌只是用户下次购买时的记忆提示，真正的壁垒是迭代速度和定义新场景的能力；对手是“试金石”，而非要消灭的目标。
对 AI 和机器人他保持克制：家庭场景的 AI 应用仍在“拿锤子找钉子”阶段；他判断机器人会像物种进化一样多形态并存，而不是都走向人形，企业应围绕具体场景深挖。
title: 155. 和科沃斯钱程聊，父与子、企二代接班的样本与肌理、机器人，和我内心的追寻

lines: Sundar Pichai says compute is the main bottleneck for frontier AI, and that Google's capacity today reflects infrastructure bets made years ago; it must split that compute between Cloud customers and its own Gemini research.
He frames recursive self-improvement as AI agents helping researchers build models in an iterative loop, not an uncontrolled intelligence explosion.
Pichai cites AI coding gains inside Google: roughly 30% more code submissions and about a third fewer rollbacks caused by errors.
On safety, he argues for defense in depth (real-time monitoring, sandboxing) and eventually independent, industry-wide audits modeled on financial controls.
Looking out 20 years, he sees interfaces shifting to agents that adapt to users, and mentions experimental ideas like space-based data centers powered by solar energy.
title: Google CEO Sundar Pichai: AI’s Infinite Possibilities, Compute Scarcity Dilemmas, Future AI Products

lines: Mercedes F1 boss Toto Wolff says cost caps have turned Formula 1 from an unlimited R&D arms race into a resource-allocation game, and teams from marketing cost centers into profitable businesses with roughly 30% EBIT margins thanks to scarce franchises and booming popularity.

He credits Drive to Survive with layering soap-opera storytelling on top of a credible, rule-based sport, pulling in new audiences such as young women; he argues that credibility is what underpins teams' multi-billion-dollar valuations.
On talent, Wolff says Mercedes scouts drivers from karting as young as eight, looking for an intuitive 'connectedness' to the car and social competence rather than physical metrics alone.
Inside the team he enforces a 'no genius asshole' rule, and before pushing regulatory gray-area innovations, engineers run 'mock trials' arguing both sides of their legality.
As an investor he stresses exiting when valuations detach from reality, and says founder transitions need the outgoing leader to stay out of day-to-day operations.
title: How Toto Wolff built the most valuable team in F1

lines: 全球流动性已经到了“存量博弈”阶段，钱不够同时撑起 AI 基建投入和各国政府扩表。
国内看 9 月金融数据：直接融资占比再次超过贷款；政府发债后不再赶进度投项目，更多用于化债和应对外部冲击；助贷和影子银行被收紧后，居民短贷出现负增长。
AI 方面，数据中心债在二级市场折价，市场从奖励“投得多”转向惩罚负自由现金流。
应对思路：节目称人民币跨境结算占比已到五成左右，贸易顺差通过 ODI 留在海外；政策引导公募均衡配置、险资持有高股息蓝筹来稳定指数。
title: Vol.238 宏观漫谈112｜全球资本市场，集体“缺钱”？

lines: OpenAI's health AI lead Karan Singhal argues AI can become a proactive "quarterback" for personal health, with 300M+ people already asking ChatGPT health questions each week.
He says training general-purpose models with medical data at every phase beats building standalone healthcare models, which quickly go stale.

Use cases he highlights: a safety net for patients in fragmented care, catching drug interactions and missed diagnoses for clinicians, and cutting the 5–17 year lag before new guidelines reach practice.

The main adoption barrier, in his view, is friction: AI must sit inside existing workflows such as EHRs; he also sees payer and provider billing bots moving from an arms race to a shared record of the encounter.
Biggest cost savings, he argues, will come from managing chronic conditions early as the price of high-level medical intelligence keeps falling.
title: What Happens When Everyone Has a Health Expert in Their Pocket? | OpenAI’s Karan Singhal

lines: 四川大学王果老师讲卢作孚如何把匪患丛生的北碚建成现代工业中心，认为这是中国本土化现代化的一个重要样本。
关键在于峡防局：原本的地方团练被改造成“寓兵于工”的现代机构，以较低成本维持治安，同时推动市政改革、煤矿开发和民众教育。
卢作孚以铁路和航运把煤炭变成工业动力，把能源中心和工业中心结合起来，并创办中国西部科学院，让科研直接服务农业、矿业生产；这些积累后来成为抗战大后方工业化的能源支撑。
嘉宾认为，和外来知识分子的乡建实验相比，本地精英依托社会网络推动的“在地工业化”更有执行力；重庆作为陪都的工业与科教基因，源自战前的系统布局，而非战争偶然。
title: 509 通往战时陪都之路：卢作孚建设重庆北碚往事

lines: CME CEO Terry Duffy argues regulators are sidestepping core principles by approving contracts open to manipulation, such as prediction markets on trivial events.
He says perpetual futures are really swaps: with no expiry and complex funding rates, they are hard for institutions to risk-manage.
He sees 24/7 trading as inevitable, but says banking and settlement infrastructure can't yet support it for big asset classes like equities, risking pockets of illiquidity.
Duffy also expects the GPU compute market to outgrow crypto by 2030 and to need futures for hedging; he calls for durable rules that survive changes of administration and equal access to market data.
title: CME's Terry Duffy on the Disconcerting State of Finance Regulation

lines: Vanta's CEO on turning a compliance-automation SaaS into an AI security platform: a "Trust Graph" of each customer's systems lets agents handle offboarding, monitoring and remediation at machine speed.
On the business model, she warns that token-based pricing invites direct comparison with raw model costs, and favors usage, retention and long-run margins over low-margin AI growth.

Other threads: agents need modular codebases, pen testing is shifting to continuous automated fixes, pay dispersion is widening for high-agency talent, and some non-US customers are diversifying away from US models.
title: Christina Cacioppo - Building an Enduring Software Company in the Age of AI - [Invest Like the Best, EP.496]

lines: Figma CEO Dylan Field argues that as AI commoditizes code, software differentiation shifts to design, brand and emotional resonance: "design is the new code."
In his view, AI lowers the floor for production but doesn't raise the ceiling; quality still depends on human intent and bold, non-consensus ideas outside models' training distribution.
On the blocked $20B Adobe deal, he says a long regulatory review can hurt innovation more than the competition it targets, by freezing companies in ambiguity.
He pushes back on the "SaaS apocalypse": vendors with deep, specialized workflows and strong UX are still growing; he also expects explicit AI disclosure to become a trust signal.
title: Dylan Field: Is AI Replacing Designers?, Design is the New Code & Democratizing Creativity
